claim: Prmt1 proteins are highly expressed in wild-type brain but significantly reduced in the brain of Prmt1+/- mice.
source: Immunoblot analysis demonstrated that Prmt1 proteins were highly expressed in wild-type (WT) brain but significantly reduced in the brain of Prmt1+/- mice (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1a comparing WT and Prmt1+/- brain tissue.

claim: Spontaneous seizure activity was observed from Prmt1+/- mice.
source: We used long-term video- electroencephalographic (EEG) recording (24 hr per day for 6 days) to monitor behavior and spontaneous EEG activity in freely moving Prmt1+/- (n = 8) and WT mice (n = 6), which led to observation of spontaneous seizure activity from Prmt1+/- mice (n = 8) (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by EEG recording data from 8 Prmt1+/- mice over 6 days, with representative traces shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: Epileptiform spikes with a delta frequency range (1–3 Hz) appeared in Prmt1+/- mice.
source: Epileptiform spikes with a delta frequency range (1–3 Hz) appeared in Prmt1 +/- mice (Figure 1d, Figure 1—source data 1), and lasted for 96.7 ± 12.5 s (range, 30–400 s, Figure 1e, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative EEG analysis showing spike frequency and duration in Prmt1+/- mice, with data presented in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Human seizures usually last less than 3 minutes.
source: These results are in parallel with human seizures that usually last less than 3 min (Bromfield EB and Sirven, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bromfield EB and Sirven, 2006.

claim: The number of seizure occurrences was 4.1 ± 1.4 per day in Prmt1+/- mice.
source: The number of seizure occurrences was 4.1 ± 1.4 per day in Prmt1+/- mice (range, 0.3–12 per day, Figure 1f, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of seizure frequency over 6 days of EEG recording, with data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Seizure activity was not observed in WT mice.
source: Seizure activity was not observed in WT mice (Figure 1d–f, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by EEG recording data from 6 WT mice showing absence of seizure activity, with data presented in Figure 1d-f.

claim: During seizure activities of Prmt1+/- mice, partial seizure behaviors (stages 1–3 seizures on the Racine scale) or no changes in behavior were typically observed.
source: During these seizure activities of Prmt1+/- mice, we typically observed partial seizure behaviors (stages 1–3 seizures on the Racine scale) or no changes in behavior (Figure 1g, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral scoring data during EEG-recorded seizures, with data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Convulsive seizures (stages 4 and 5) were rarely observed in Prmt1+/- mice.
source: Convulsive seizures (stages 4 and 5) were rarely observed in Prmt1+/- mice (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by behavioral scoring data showing low frequency of severe seizures, with data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Behavioral hyperactivity, such as an increase in open-field locomotion, frequently accompanies seizures.
source: Behavioral hyperactivity, such as an increase in open-field locomotion, frequently accompanies seizures (Kim et al., 2011; Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Peters et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2011; Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Peters et al., 2005.

claim: Male Prmt1+/- mutants showed a slight increase in locomotor activity.
source: In an open-field test, male mutants showed a slight increase in locomotor activity (Figure 1h–j, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by open-field test data from 10 Prmt1+/- and 9 WT mice, with results shown in Figure 1h-j.

claim: The Prmt1+/- mice spent a similar amount of time in the center of the open-field box compared with the control mice.
source: The Prmt1+/- mice (n = 10) spent a similar amount of time in the center of the open-field box compared with the control mice (n = 9) (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by open-field test data measuring time in center zone, with results shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The Prmt1+/- mice moved a longer distance than WT mice.
source: However, the Prmt1+/- mice moved a longer distance than WT mice (Figure 1i).
evidence: Supported by open-field test data measuring total distance traveled, with results shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The total travel distance was increased significantly in Prmt1+/- mice, compared to that in WT mice (p<0.05).
source: The total travel distance was increased significantly in Prmt1+/- mice, compared to that in WT mice (p<0.05; Figure 1j).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of open-field test data showing significant difference (p<0.05), with results shown in Figure 1j.

claim: Prmt1+/- mice display signs of a persistent neuronal hyperexcitability, including spontaneous seizures and a slightly increased locomotor activity.
source: Thus, Prmt1+/- mice display signs of a persistent neuronal hyperexcitability, including spontaneous seizures and a slightly increased locomotor activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined EEG and behavioral data showing seizures and increased locomotion in Prmt1+/- mice.

claim: Hyperexcitability of hippocampal neurons is a characteristic feature of most epilepsies.
source: Hyperexcitability of hippocampal neurons is a characteristic feature of most epilepsies (Noebels, 2003; McCormick and Contreras, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Noebels, 2003; McCormick and Contreras, 2001.

claim: GCs from WT mice typically displayed tonic firing patterns in response to a 1-s square current pulse injection.
source: GCs from WT mice typically displayed tonic firing patterns in response to a 1-s square current pulse injection: AP frequency elevated as the magnitude of the square pulse increased (Figure 2a and c, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data from 16 WT granule cells, with representative traces shown in Figure 2a and c.

claim: GCs from Prmt1+/- mice showed significantly higher AP frequency than those from WT mice.
source: GCs from Prmt1+/- mice showed significantly higher AP frequency than those from WT mice (Figure 2b and c, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data from 18 Prmt1+/- granule cells compared to 16 WT cells, with results shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The averaged AP frequency in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current in WT GCs was 8.1 ± 1.4 Hz (n = 16), while it increased significantly to 31.2 ± 2.2 Hz (n = 18, p<0.01) in Prmt1+/- GCs.
source: The averaged AP frequency in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current in WT GCs was 8.1 ± 1.4 Hz (n = 16), while it increased significantly to 31.2 ± 2.2 Hz (n = 18, p<0.01) in Prmt1+/- GCs (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of action potential frequency from current-clamp recordings, with statistical significance p<0.01, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The heterozygous deletion of the Prmt1 gene enhanced excitability of hippocampal neurons.
source: These data indicate that the heterozygous deletion of the Prmt1 gene enhanced excitability of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the increased action potential frequency observed in Prmt1+/- granule cells compared to WT.

claim: The current for spike initiation was reduced in Prmt1+/- neurons.
source: Representative traces in Figure 2d,e clearly show that the current for spike initiation was reduced in Prmt1+/- neurons.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data showing threshold current measurements, with representative traces in Figure 2d and e.

claim: Analysis of pooled results revealed a significant decrease in the mean threshold current in Prmt1+/- GCs compared to that in WT GCs.
source: Analysis of pooled results revealed a significant decrease in the mean threshold current in Prmt1+/- GCs compared to that in WT GCs (Figure 2f, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of threshold current measurements from multiple cells, with results shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The change in threshold current was correlated with an increase in the input resistance.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2g, the change in threshold current was correlated with an increase in the input resistance.
evidence: Supported by input resistance measurements from current-clamp recordings, with results shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The amplitude and duration of APs obtained in WT were not altered by the reduction of the Prmt1 gene dose.
source: The amplitude and duration of APs obtained in WT were not altered by the reduction of the Prmt1 gene dose (Figure 2h and i, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of action potential properties showing no significant difference in amplitude or half-width, with results shown in Figure 2h and i.

claim: The change in the threshold current in Prmt1+/- neurons reflects the effect on input resistance, which facilitates their AP initiation and, hence, increase in spike number.
source: Therefore, the change in the threshold current in Prmt1+/- neurons reflects the effect on input resistance, which facilitates their AP initiation and, hence, increase in spike number.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of decreased threshold current, increased input resistance, and increased spike number in Prmt1+/- neurons.

claim: An increase in neuronal excitability without a change in AP height and width indicated that the kinetics and amplitude of voltage-gated currents associated with the spike itself were not affected.
source: An increase in neuronal excitability without a change in AP height and width indicated that the kinetics and amplitude of voltage-gated currents associated with the spike itself were not affected.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AP amplitude and duration were unchanged despite increased excitability.

claim: Increased cation current or leak current was unlikely to be involved in the phenotype, as this would be expected to result in a decrease in input resistance.
source: Increased cation current or leak current was unlikely to be involved in the phenotype, either, as this would be expected to result in a decrease in input resistance.
evidence: Based on established knowledge that increased leak currents decrease input resistance, which is opposite to the observed increase.

claim: The most probable target was the KCNQ/M channel.
source: Thus, the most probable target was the KCNQ/M channel.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of increased excitability and input resistance, which is consistent with KCNQ channel dysfunction.

claim: Inhibiting the KCNQ channel increases both input resistance and neuronal excitability.
source: KCNQs are voltage-dependent K+ channels that partially open at the resting membrane potential. Inhibiting the KCNQ channel increases both input resistance and neuronal excitability (Jentsch, 2000; Brown and Passmore, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jentsch, 2000; Brown and Passmore, 2009.

claim: In GCs from WT mice, a step to -60 mV forced deactivation of a slowly relaxing outward current that decayed, consistent with the presence of M-current.
source: In GCs from WT mice, a step to -60 mV forced deactivation of a slowly relaxing outward current that decayed, consistent with the presence of M-current.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data from WT granule cells showing characteristic M-current deactivation kinetics.

claim: The M-channel antagonist XE991 (10 μM) caused a complete loss of detectable M-current.
source: The M-channel antagonist XE991 (10 μM) caused a complete loss of detectable M-current (Figure 3a), accompanied by a reduction in the holding current.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data showing elimination of M-current upon XE991 application, with representative traces in Figure 3a.

claim: Prmt1+/- GCs showed little measurable M-currents (p<0.001).
source: However, Prmt1+/- GCs showed little measurable M-currents (p<0.001) (Figure 3b–c, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data from 12 Prmt1+/- granule cells showing significantly reduced M-current compared to 22 WT cells (p<0.001), with results shown in Figure 3b-c.

claim: XE991 application led to a depolarization (ΔVm, 4.5 ± 1.6 mV) in WT neurons.
source: Consistent with the major contribution of the KCNQ channel (Delmas and Brown, 2005), XE991 application led to a depolarization (ΔVm, 4.5 ± 1.6 mV) in WT neurons.
evidence: Supported by membrane potential measurements before and after XE991 application in WT neurons.

claim: The effect of XE991 on membrane potential was abolished in the mutant (ΔVm, −0.9 ± 0.7 mV).
source: In contrast, such an effect of XE991 was abolished in the mutant (ΔVm, −0.9 ± 0.7 mV) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by membrane potential measurements before and after XE991 application in Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Application of XE991 increased input resistance in the WT neurons (Δinput resistance, 51.7 ± 4.6 MΩ) but had less of an effect in the mutant (Δinput resistance, 29.2 ± 6.3 MΩ).
source: Similarly, application of XE991 increased input resistance in the WT neurons (Δinput resistance, 51.7 ± 4.6 MΩ) but had less of an effect in the mutant (Δinput resistance, 29.2 ± 6.3 MΩ) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by input resistance measurements before and after XE991 application in WT and Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The Prmt1+/- neurons' threshold currents were also insensitive to XE991 treatment.
source: The Prmt1+/- neurons' threshold currents were also insensitive to XE991 treatment (Figure 3e, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by threshold current measurements before and after XE991 application in Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The increase in the input resistance of Prmt1+/- neurons might be a result of the reduced level of KCNQ channel activity.
source: These results suggest that the increase in the input resistance of Prmt1+/- neurons might be a result of the reduced level of KCNQ channel activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Prmt1+/- neurons have reduced M-currents and increased input resistance that is insensitive to XE991.

claim: The firing frequency in WT neurons increased significantly after applying 10 μM XE991.
source: We further examined the effect of XE991 on firing frequency. The firing frequency in WT neurons increased significantly after applying 10 μM XE991 (Delmas and Brown, 2005) (Figure 3f, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data showing increased action potential frequency upon XE991 application in WT neurons, with results shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The AP frequency in response to a 200 pA-depolarizing current was 8.4 ± 1.9 Hz in the control and increased to 12.6 ± 1.9 Hz following the application of 10 μM XE991.
source: For example, the AP frequency in response to a 200 pA-depolarizing current was 8.4 ± 1.9 Hz in the control and increased to 12.6 ± 1.9 Hz following the application of 10 μM XE991.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of action potential frequency before and after XE991 application in WT neurons.

claim: XE991-induced spiking was largely absent in the mutant neurons.
source: This XE991-induced spiking was largely absent in the mutant neurons (Figure 3g, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data showing minimal change in firing frequency upon XE991 application in Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Before and after the XE991 treatment, AP frequency in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current was 34 ± 3.2 Hz and 35.2 ± 5.6 Hz, respectively, in Prmt1+/- neurons.
source: Before and after the XE991 treatment, AP frequency in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current was 34 ± 3.2 Hz and 35.2 ± 5.6 Hz, respectively.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of action potential frequency before and after XE991 application in Prmt1+/- neurons.

claim: Prmt1+/- GCs displayed a high firing rate at baseline, and their firings did not further increase during XE-991 application, suggesting that defective M-current contributes to the neuronal hyperexcitability observed in the Prmt1+/- mice.
source: Thus, these results showed that Prmt1+/- GCs displayed a high firing rate at baseline, and their firings did not further increase during XE-991 application, suggesting that defective M-current contributes to the neuronal hyperexcitability observed in the Prmt1+/- mice.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that Prmt1+/- neurons have high baseline firing, reduced M-currents, and insensitivity to XE991.

claim: The potential involvement of other Prmt1 target(s) in the neuronal hyperexcitability observed in the Prmt1+/- mice cannot be excluded.
source: However, we cannot exclude the potential involvement of other Prmt1 target(s) in the neuronal hyperexcitability observed in the Prmt1+/- mice.
evidence: Speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the study and possibility of additional mechanisms.

claim: The treatment of WT hippocampal slices with MTA (100 μM) or furamidine dihydrochloride (20 μM) for 1 hr completely abolished M-currents.
source: The treatment of WT hippocampal slices with MTA (100 μM) or furamidine dihydrochloride (20 μM) for 1 hr completely abolished M-currents (Figure 4a–c; p<0.001 vs WT control, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data from WT granule cells treated with methyltransferase inhibitors, with results shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: The application of MTA (100 μM, 1 hr) enhanced neuronal excitability of WT GCs.
source: We then studied their effects on neuronal excitability. The application of MTA (100 μM, 1 hr) enhanced neuronal excitability of WT GCs (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data showing increased firing frequency in MTA-treated WT neurons, with results shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: After the MTA treatment, AP frequency in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current was 34.7 ± 4.6 Hz.
source: After the MTA treatment, AP frequency in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current was 34.7 ± 4.6 Hz.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of action potential frequency in MTA-treated WT neurons.

claim: Subsequent application of XE991 had no further effect on firing frequency after MTA treatment (AP frequency was 31.8 ± 3.9 Hz).
source: Consistent with ablation of M-currents by MTA, subsequent application of XE991 had no further effect (AP frequency was 31.8 ± 3.9 Hz) (Figure 4d–e, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data showing no additional change in firing frequency upon XE991 application after MTA treatment, with results shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: The MTA-induced increase in excitability was accompanied by the declined AP threshold currents and increased input resistance.
source: The MTA-induced increase in excitability was accompanied by the declined AP threshold currents and increased input resistance (threshold current, 110.5 ± 5.5 pA, n = 4; input resistance, 234.0 ± 5.8 MΩ, n = 4), which were relatively insensitive to a subsequential treatment with XE991 (p>0.05; Figure 4j–k, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements of threshold current and input resistance in MTA-treated WT neurons before and after XE991 application, with results shown in Figure 4j-k.

claim: The treatment of WT hippocampal slices with furamidine dihydrochloride exhibited a similar effect on neuronal excitability, input resistance, and threshold current.
source: Furthermore, the treatment of WT hippocampal slices with furamidine dihydrochloride exhibited a similar effect on neuronal excitability, input resistance, and threshold current, confirming the results obtained with MTA treatment (Figure 4f–g and j–k, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data from furamidine-treated WT neurons showing similar effects as MTA treatment, with results shown in Figure 4f-g and j-k.

claim: Methylation suppression with MTA had no effect on AP firing, threshold current, or input resistance in Prmt1+/- GCs.
source: However, methylation suppression with MTA had no effect on AP firing (Figure 4h–i, Figure 4—source data 1), threshold current (Figure 4j, Figure 4—source data 1), or input resistance (Figure 4k, Figure 4—source data 1) in Prmt1+/- GCs.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recording data from MTA-treated Prmt1+/- neurons showing no change in excitability parameters, with results shown in Figure 4h-k.

claim: The reduction of Prmt1 activity in the hippocampal neurons might be responsible for the neuronal hyperexcitability in Prmt1+/- neurons.
source: Thus, these data suggest that the reduction of Prmt1 activity in the hippocampal neurons might be responsible for the neuronal hyperexcitability in Prmt1+/- neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pharmacological inhibition of Prmt1 in WT neurons phenocopies the hyperexcitability of Prmt1+/- neurons.

claim: KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 protein levels were unchanged in hippocampi from Prmt1+/- mice.
source: Importantly, KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 protein levels were unchanged in hippocampi from Prmt1+/- mice, suggesting the involvement of post-translational mechanisms in the regulation of KCNQ currents (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 protein levels in WT and Prmt1+/- hippocampal lysates, with results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: KCNQ2 and Prmt1 proteins were coprecipitated when co-expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: KCNQ2 and Prmt1 proteins were coprecipitated when co-expressed in HEK293T cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEK293T cells, with results shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The intracellular C-terminal region of KCNQ2 encompassing amino acids 320–840, designated as KCNQ2-C, was sufficient to interact with Prmt1.
source: The intracellular C-terminal region of KCNQ2 encompassing amino acids 320–840, designated as KCNQ2-C, was sufficient to interact with Prmt1 (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using KCNQ2-C construct, with results shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: KCNQ2 was co-immunoprecipitated endogenously with Prmt1 in hippocampus.
source: To further confirm the interaction between KCNQ2 and Prmt1 proteins in the native neuronal environment, co-immunoprecipitation was performed with mouse hippocampal lysates. We found that KCNQ2 was co-immunoprecipitated endogenously with Prmt1 in hippocampus (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using mouse hippocampal lysates, with results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Four arginine residues such as Arg333 (R333), Arg345 (R345), Arg353 (R353), and Arg435 (R435), were identified as methylated in vivo.
source: To assess whether KCNQ2 is methylated in vivo and to identify the in vivo methylation sites, we performed a liquid-chromatography-coupled tandem mass spectrometric analysis. Four arginine residues such as Arg333 (R333), Arg345 (R345), Arg353 (R353), and Arg435 (R435), were identified as methylated in vivo (Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of KCNQ2 protein, with methylated peptides identified and shown in Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: GST-KCNQ2 was methylated by Prmt1, but not by other Prmts.
source: To determine whether Prmt1 methylates KCNQ2, we performed in vitro methylation assays using various bacterially purified GST-Prmts (Prmt1-6) or myc-tagged Prmt5 purified from HEK293T cells and GST-KCNQ2 (amino acids 320–449) that contain all of four arginine residues identified by mass spectrometry. GST-KCNQ2 was methylated by Prmt1, but not by other Prmts (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by in vitro methylation assays using purified recombinant proteins and radioactive SAM, with results shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Substitution of the four Arg's in KCNQ2 (4RK, R333K/R345K/R353K/R435K) completely abolished the methylation by Prmt1.
source: Furthermore, substitution of the four Arg's in KCNQ2 (4RK, R333K/R345K/R353K/R435K) completely abolished the methylation by Prmt1, suggesting that these four arginine residues are critical targets for Prmt1-dependent methylation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro methylation assays using KCNQ2 mutants, showing loss of methylation signal with 4RK mutant.

claim: Prmt1 knockdown specifically decreased the ADMA-positive KCNQ2 levels.
source: To test whether Prmt1 methylates KCNQ2 in vivo, HEK293T cells expressing HA-KCNQ2 were transfected with control or Prmt1 shRNA, followed by immunoprecipitation with anti-KCNQ2 antibodies and immunoblotting with antibodies to asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) and KCNQ2. Prmt1 knockdown specifically decreased the ADMA-positive KCNQ2 levels, suggesting that KCNQ2 methylation is sensitive to Prmt1 levels (Figure 5g).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis showing reduced ADMA signal on KCNQ2 upon Prmt1 knockdown, with results shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Prmt1 overexpression enhanced KCNQ2 methylation.
source: Conversely, Prmt1 overexpression enhanced KCNQ2 methylation (Figure 5h).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis showing increased ADMA signal on KCNQ2 upon Prmt1 overexpression, with results shown in Figure 5h.

claim: ADMA-positive KCNQ2 proteins were readily detected in the WT brain, which were significantly reduced in that of Prmt1+/-.
source: We next examined the arginine methylation status of KCNQ2 channels in WT or Prmt1+/- brains (Figure 5i). The immunoprecipitation analysis showed that ADMA-positive KCNQ2 proteins were readily detected in the WT brain, which were significantly reduced in that of Prmt1+/-.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis of brain lysates from WT and Prmt1+/- mice, with results shown in Figure 5i.

claim: Prmt1 interacts with and methylates KCNQ2.
source: These results strongly advocate that Prmt1 interacts with and methylates KCNQ2.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of co-immunoprecipitation, in vitro methylation assays, and in vivo methylation analysis.

claim: The protein expression of Prmt8 in the Prmt1+/- brain was unaltered from WT brain.
source: Prmt1 and Prmt8 often share substrates in vitro, and PRMT8 is neuron-specific (Kousaka et al., 2009). We analyzed whether Prmt8 contributes to hypo-methylation of KCNQ2 proteins in Prmt1+/- brains. The protein expression of Prmt8 in the Prmt1+/- brain was unaltered from WT brain (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of Prmt8 protein levels in WT and Prmt1+/- brain lysates, with results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Prmt8 might not be involved in the decreased KCNQ2 methylation in Prmt1+/- brain.
source: Thus, Prmt8 might not be involved in the decreased KCNQ2 methylation in Prmt1+/- brain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Prmt8 levels are unchanged in Prmt1+/- brain despite reduced KCNQ2 methylation.

claim: Reduced Prmt1 levels cause hypo-methylation of KCNQ2 in the Prmt1+/- brain.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that reduced Prmt1 levels cause hypo-methylation of KCNQ2 in the Prmt1+/- brain.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that Prmt1+/- brains have reduced Prmt1 levels and reduced KCNQ2 methylation, while Prmt8 levels are unchanged.

claim: The shRNA-mediated depletion of Prmt1 decreased KCNQ current density from 57.6 ± 7.6 pA/pF of control transfected cells to 26.3 ± 7.6 pA/pF.
source: The shRNA-mediated depletion of Prmt1 decreased KCNQ current density from 57.6 ± 7.6 pA/pF of control transfected cells to 26.3 ± 7. 6 pA/pF.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing KCNQ2 with or without Prmt1 knockdown.

claim: Rectification of the I-V curves was not changed by Prmt1 knockdown.
source: Rectification of the I-V curves was not changed by Prmt1 knockdown.
evidence: Supported by analysis of current-voltage relationships from whole-cell patch clamp recordings.

claim: The treatment of MTA or furamidine dramatically reduced the KCNQ2 currents.
source: To verify the role of Prmt1-mediated methylation in KCNQ2 channel function, the effect of Prmt1 inhibitors on KCNQ2 current was examined. In agreement with Prmt1 knockdown data, the treatment of MTA or furamidine dramatically reduced the KCNQ2 currents (Figure 6c–d, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing KCNQ2 treated with methyltransferase inhibitors, with results shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: 100 μM MTA or 20 μM furamidine inhibited KCNQ2 currents by 79.9 ± 13.6% and 72.1 ± 2.1%, respectively.
source: The KCNQ2 currents were confirmed by XE991 treatment. Assuming that the XE991-sensitive portion entirely represents KCNQ2 currents, 100 μM MTA or 20 μM furamidine inhibited KCNQ2 currents by 79.9 ± 13.6% and 72.1 ± 2.1%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of KCNQ2 current inhibition by methyltransferase inhibitors, using XE991-sensitive current as reference.

claim: KCNQ2 mutants with reduced methylation exhibited remarkably decreased KCNQ2 currents compared to WT.
source: We further examined the correlation between the Prmt1-induced methylation and KCNQ2 channel function by recording whole-cell currents in HEK293T cells expressing WT or KCNQ2 mutants. Compared to WT, the KCNQ2 mutants with reduced methylation exhibited remarkably decreased KCNQ2 currents (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing WT or mutant KCNQ2 channels, with representative traces shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The current density at +40 mV was 304.4 ± 11.0 pA/pF (n = 5) for WT KCNQ2 channels.
source: The current density at +40 mV was 304.4 ± 11.0 pA/pF (n = 5) for WT KCNQ2 channels.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of steady-state current density from whole-cell patch clamp recordings.

claim: Significantly decreased KCNQ2 currents were observed in cells expressing RK mutants (R333K, R345K, R353K, R435K, or 4RK).
source: We observed significantly decreased KCNQ2 currents in cells expressing RK mutants (R333K, R345K, R353K, R435K, or 4RK): in these cells the current density (pA/pF) of steady-state currents at +40 mV were 18.2 ± 0.3 (n = 3, p<0.001), 13.7 ± 0.5 (n = 3, p<0.001), 14.8 ± 3.9 (n = 3, p<0.001), 18.0 ± 2.2 (n = 4, p<0.001), and 12.5 ± 1.6 (n = 4, p<0.001), respectively (Figure 6f, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of current density from whole-cell patch clamp recordings of mutant KCNQ2 channels, with statistical significance p<0.001, and results shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The arginine methylation of KCNQ2 is required for its channel activity.
source: These data suggest that the arginine methylation of KCNQ2 is required for its channel activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutations preventing methylation dramatically reduce KCNQ2 current.

claim: KCNQ2 mutants showed no alteration in sensitivity to retigabine, KCNQ channel activator.
source: Importantly, KCNQ2 mutants showed no alteration in sensitivity to retigabine, KCNQ channel activator (Figure 9d–g, summary data in Figure 9i, Figure 9—source data 1), indicating that methylation regulates channel function through a distinct molecular mechanism not overall potential of channel activation.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings showing similar retigabine-induced current augmentation in WT and mutant KCNQ2 channels, with results shown in Figure 9d-g and i.

claim: The ratio of channels on the membrane to those in the total lysates was not significantly different between control cells and Prmt1 knockdown cells.
source: To assess whether methylation of KCNQ2 regulates its cell surface localization, we labeled total plasma membrane proteins of intact cells with membrane-impermeable biotinylation reagents, and isolated membrane proteins with streptavidin beads. The ratio of channels on the membrane to those in the total lysates was not significantly different between control cells and Prmt1 knockdown cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, left panel).
evidence: Supported by surface biotinylation assays comparing membrane and total KCNQ2 levels in control and Prmt1 knockdown cells, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: KCNQ2-4RK showed a similar amount of biotinylation when expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: KCNQ2-4RK also showed a similar amount of biotinylation when expressed in HEK293T cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, right panel).
evidence: Supported by surface biotinylation assays showing similar membrane localization of 4RK mutant compared to WT, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: As the surface-resident channels remained unchanged, the KCNQ conductance should be determined by the open probability.
source: As the surface-resident channels remained unchanged, the KCNQ conductance should be determined by the open probability.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that surface expression is unchanged despite reduced current, suggesting changes in channel gating rather than trafficking.

claim: KCNQ/M channels require a certain level of PIP2 in the cell membrane to maintain their activity.
source: KCNQ/M channels require a certain level of PIP2 in the cell membrane to maintain their activity (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Suh and Hille, 2002; Winks et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delmas and Brown, 2005; Suh and Hille, 2002; Winks et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2003.

claim: PIP2 acts to stabilize the open state of KCNQ2 channels resulting in increased open probability at all voltage levels.
source: PIP2 acts to stabilize the open state of KCNQ2 channels resulting in increased open probability at all voltage levels.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PIP2 regulation of KCNQ channels.

claim: The depletion of PIP2 or the reduction of PIP2 affinity of channel can suppress KCNQ currents.
source: Thus, the depletion of PIP2 (Suh and Hille, 2002; Winks et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2003) or the reduction of PIP2 affinity of channel (Kosenko et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Hernandez et al., 2008) can suppress KCNQ currents.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing PIP2 dependence of KCNQ channels.

claim: The methylated arginine residues, R333, R345, R353, and R435, reside in the PIP2-binding domain of KCNQ2.
source: Interestingly, the methylated arginine residues, R333, R345, R353, and R435, reside in the PIP2-binding domain of KCNQ2 (Suh and Hille, 2008; Hernandez et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on known structural information about KCNQ2 PIP2-binding domain from cited studies.

claim: Methylation might affect the PIP2 binding affinity of KCNQ2 thereby regulating channel activities.
source: This led us to postulate that methylation might affect the PIP2 binding affinity of KCNQ2 thereby regulating channel activities.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the location of methylation sites within the PIP2-binding domain.

claim: Neomycin is widely used to sequester PIP2.
source: To appraise the affinity of PIP2 for KCNQ2, we utilized neomycin, which is widely used to sequester PIP2 (Liscovitch et al., 1994; Haider et al., 2007; Suh and Hille, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liscovitch et al., 1994; Haider et al., 2007; Suh and Hille, 2007.

claim: Neomycin is a polycation that binds specifically to PIP2.
source: Since neomycin is a polycation that binds specifically to PIP2, it has been used to determine the PIP2 content in biological membranes (Arbuzova et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arbuzova et al., 2000.

claim: The neomycin sensitivity of ion channels such as Kir and KCNQ is well regarded as a measure of its PIP2 affinity.
source: The neomycin sensitivity of ion channels such as Kir and KCNQ is well regarded as a measure of its PIP2 affinity (Haider et al., 2007; Suh and Hille, 2007; Kosenko et al., 2012; Schulze et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haider et al., 2007; Suh and Hille, 2007; Kosenko et al., 2012; Schulze et al., 2003.

claim: Ion channels with high PIP2 affinities are expected to be less sensitive to neomycin than those with low PIP2 affinity.
source: Accordingly, ion channels with high PIP2 affinities are expected to be less sensitive to neomycin than those with low PIP2 affinity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of neomycin-PIP2 competition mechanism.

claim: Inclusion of 10 μM neomycin in the patch pipette solution led to a moderate inhibition of the WT KCNQ2 current in HEK293T cells.
source: Inclusion of 10 μM neomycin in the patch pipette solution led to a moderate inhibition of the WT KCNQ2 current in HEK293T cells (Figure 7a, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings with neomycin in the pipette solution, with results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Mutant channels with reduced methylation showed greatly increased inhibition by 10 mM neomycin.
source: In contrast, mutant channels with reduced methylation showed greatly increased inhibition by 10 mM neomycin.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings comparing neomycin sensitivity of WT and mutant KCNQ2 channels.

claim: The remaining current at 10 min time points after rupturing the membrane is significantly reduced from 81.2 ± 1.9% (WT, n = 5) to 48.7 ± 4.2% (R333K, n = 5, p<0.01).
source: So, the remaining current at 10 min time points after rupturing the membrane is significantly reduced from 81.2 ± 1.9% (WT, n = 5) to 48.7 ± 4.2% (R333K, n = 5, p<0.01; Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of neomycin-induced current rundown, with statistical significance p<0.01, and results shown in Figure 7a.

claim: In comparison with WT, methylation-deficient mutant KCNQ2 (R333K, R345K, R353K, R435K) exhibited a higher sensitivity to neomycin.
source: We measured dose-responses to neomycin. In comparison with WT, methylation-deficient mutant KCNQ2 (R333K, R345K, R353K, R435K) exhibited a higher sensitivity to neomycin (Figure 7b, Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting lower PIP2 affinity.
evidence: Supported by dose-response analysis of neomycin sensitivity showing leftward shift in IC50 for mutant channels, with results shown in Figure 7b.

claim: WT KCNQ2 did not show increase in current by diC8-PIP2 even at 200 μM, suggesting that endogenous PIP2 might be at a saturating concentration.
source: WT KCNQ2 did not show increase in current by diC8-PIP2 even at 200 μM, suggesting that endogenous PIP2 might be at a saturating concentration.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings with exogenous PIP2 in the pipette solution, showing no current augmentation in WT channels.

claim: Methylation-deficient mutant KCNQ2 (R333K, R345K, R353K, R435K, 4RK) showed a dose-dependent increase in current with exogenous PIP2.
source: In contrast, methylation-deficient mutant KCNQ2 (R333K, R345K, R353K, R435K, 4RK) showed a dose-dependent increase in current but they did not reach to WT level at corresponding concentrations of PIP2.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings with varying concentrations of exogenous PIP2 in the pipette solution.

claim: Only R333K reached to the WT level when introduced to 200 μM PIP2.
source: Only R333K reached to the WT level when introduced to 200 μM PIP2.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of current density with 200 μM PIP2, showing R333K mutant current restored to WT level.

claim: 4RK appeared to be most severely affected in PIP2 binding.
source: On the other hand, 4RK appeared to be most severely affected in PIP2 binding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 4RK mutant showed the least rescue by exogenous PIP2.

claim: Activation of Dr-VSP reduced WT KCNQ2 currents and currents were recovered quickly after PIP2 resynthesis on repolarization.
source: Altered PIP2 affinity in RK mutants was also assessed by a voltage-sensitive phosphatase from Danio rerio (Dr-VSP), which hydrolyzes PIP2 at highly depolarized voltages (e.g., +100 mV) and transiently reduces the PIP2 level (Falkenburger et al., 2010; Rjasanow et al., 2015). Dr-VSP was coexpressed with WT KCNQ2 or RK mutants and its activity was elicited by membrane depolarization. Consistent with a previous report (Falkenburger et al., 2010), activation of Dr-VSP reduced WT KCNQ2 currents and currents were recovered quickly after PIP2 resynthesis on repolarization (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings using Dr-VSP to deplete PIP2, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: When subjecting RK mutants to the same VSP activation protocol, the overall behavior was similar to the WT KCNQ2 channel; however, the recovery of current was slowed 2–4 folds.
source: When subjecting RK mutants to the same VSP activation protocol, the overall behavior was similar to the WT KCNQ2 channel; however, the recovery of current was slowed 2–4 folds (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of current recovery kinetics after Dr-VSP activation, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mean time to the 70% maximum current (T70) for R333K, R345K, R353K and R435K was 22.8 ± 3.7, 24.1 ± 1.9, 32.1 ± 2.6, and 17.9 ± 1.5 s, respectively (p<0.05 vs WT:9.5 ± 3.1 s).
source: The mean time to the 70% maximum current (T70) for R333K, R345K, R353K and R435Kwas 22.8 ± 3.7, 24.1 ± 1.9, 32.1 ± 2.6, and 17.9 ± 1.5 s, respectively (p<0.05 vs WT:9.5 ± 3.1 s).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of recovery kinetics from Dr-VSP experiments, with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: The slowed recovery after VSP reflects the reduced PIP2 affinity.
source: The slowed recovery after VSP reflects the reduced PIP2 affinity (Rjasanow et al., 2015), further supporting for the reduced PIP2 affinity of RK mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of slowed recovery kinetics in mutants, with support from citation to Rjasanow et al., 2015.

claim: Methylation of KCNQ2 channel regulates its interaction with PIP2.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that methylation of KCNQ2 channel regulates its interaction with PIP2.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of neomycin sensitivity, exogenous PIP2 rescue, and Dr-VSP experiments.

claim: M-current density in Prmt1+/- neurons was restored to the WT level by PIP2 loading.
source: We then tested whether PIP2 loading could also rescue M-currents in neurons of Prmt1 +/- mice. As shown in Figure 7h,M-current density in Prmt1+/- neurons was restored to the WT level by PIP2 loading.
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recordings from Prmt1+/- granule cells with exogenous PIP2 in the pipette, with results shown in Figure 7h.

claim: Introduction of 20 and 200 μM diC8-PIP2 to Prmt1+/- GCs increased M-currents to 27.3 ± 2.9 (n = 3) and 29.9 ± 5.9 pA (n = 5), respectively, which are insignificantly different from that of WT (31.65 ± 2.03 pA, n = 22, p>0.05).
source: Introduction of 20 and 200 μM diC8-PIP2 to Prmt1+/- GCs increased M-currents to 27.3 ± 2.9 (n = 3) and 29.9 ± 5.9 pA (n = 5), respectively, which are insignificantly different from that of WT (31.65 ± 2.03 pA, n = 22, p>0.05; Figure 7h, Figure 7—source data 1), while exogenous PIP2 had little effects on M-currents in WT GCs (p>0.05, Figure 7h, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of M-current density with exogenous PIP2, showing restoration to WT levels in Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 7h.

claim: The input resistance decreased significantly from 214.8 ± 7.7 MΩ to 163.8 ± 16.4 MΩ upon PIP2 loading in Prmt1+/- neurons.
source: As expected from opening of the M-channels by PIP2, the input resistance decreased significantly from 214.8 ± 7.7 MΩ to 163.8 ± 16.4 MΩ (Figure 7i, Figure 7—source data 1), and the AP threshold current increased from 115.6 ± 3.3 pA to 175 ± 12.1 pA (Figure 7j, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings from Prmt1+/- granule cells with exogenous PIP2, with results shown in Figure 7i and j.

claim: Declined methylation caused by Prmt1 depletion impairs KCNQ channel activity via reduction in channel-PIP2 interaction.
source: These results indicate that declined methylation caused by Prmt1 depletion impairs KCNQ channel activity via reduction in channel-PIP2 interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PIP2 loading rescues M-currents and excitability in Prmt1+/- neurons.

claim: PIP2 loading decreased the firing rate toward normal values in Prmt1+/- GCs.
source: Since PIP2 restored the diminished KCNQ currents, we asked whether PIP2 could also reduce the observed neuronal hyperexcitability in Prmt1+/- neurons. We found that PIP2 loading decreased the firing rate toward normal values in Prmt1+/- GCs.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing reduced action potential frequency in Prmt1+/- neurons with exogenous PIP2.

claim: The AP frequency of Prmt1+/- GCs in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current was 31.2 ± 2.2 Hz, and decreased to 15.5 ± 2.9 Hz following PIP2 loading.
source: For example, the AP frequency of Prmt1+/- GCs in response to a 200 pA depolarizing current was 31.2 ± 2.2 Hz, and decreased to 15.5 ± 2.9 Hz following PIP2 loading (Figure 7k, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of action potential frequency before and after PIP2 loading in Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 7k.

claim: Prmt1+/- neurons regained the sensitivity to XE991 after PIP2 loading.
source: In addition, Prmt1+/- neurons also regained the sensitivity to XE991 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Figure 7—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing XE991-induced changes in excitability after PIP2 loading in Prmt1+/- neurons, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: PIP2 application had little effects on the excitabilities of WT neurons.
source: In contrast, PIP2 application had little effects on the excitabilities of WT neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 4, Figure 7—figure supplement 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings showing minimal changes in excitability parameters with PIP2 loading in WT neurons, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The impaired KCNQ channel function in the hippocampus of Prmt1+/- mice can be restored by PIP2 addition.
source: These results suggest that the impaired KCNQ channel function in the hippocampus of Prmt1+/- mice can be restored by PIP2 addition.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that PIP2 loading rescues M-currents and excitability in Prmt1+/- neurons.

claim: The recovery of excitability with PIP2 application was significant but incomplete, suggesting the possible involvement of other Prmt1 target(s) in neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: Although the recovery of excitability with PIP2 application was significant it was incomplete, suggesting the possible involvement of other Prmt1 target(s) in neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PIP2 loading does not fully restore excitability to WT levels.

claim: The data obtained by using apamin and paxilline ruled out that the contribution of SK and BK channels in hyperexcitability of Prmt1-deficient GCs.
source: As immediate candidates, we tested other K+ channels such as SK and BK channels in Prmt1 effects which are known to regulate membrane excitability of dentate gyrus GCs (Brenner et al., 2005). The data obtained by using apamin and paxilline, specific SK and BK channel blockers, respectively, ruled out that the contribution of these channels in hyperexcitability of Prmt1-deficient GCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 5, Figure 7—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings using SK and BK channel blockers, with results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of Prmt1 reduces the affinity between the KCNQ channel and PIP2, leading to reduction of KCNQ currents accompanied by neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: Taken together, genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of Prmt1 reduces the affinity between the KCNQ channel and PIP2, leading to reduction of KCNQ currents accompanied by neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of genetic and pharmacological experiments showing reduced PIP2 affinity, reduced M-currents, and increased excitability.

claim: Prmt1 seems to play a key role in physiological functions of KCNQ channels by controlling its interaction with PIP2 at the basal state.
source: Prmt1 seems to play a key role in physiological functions of KCNQ channels by controlling its interaction with PIP2 at the basal state.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing that Prmt1 methylation regulates KCNQ-PIP2 interaction and channel activity.

claim: KCNQ channels contribute to cellular protections in pathologic condition.
source: KCNQ channels are also known to contribute to cellular protections in pathologic condition.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of KCNQ channel function in neuroprotection.

claim: The enhancement of KCNQ currents in response to oxidative stress led to a dramatic reduction of the AP firing frequency that may prevent neuronal death.
source: In particular, the enhancement of KCNQ currents in response to oxidative stress led to a dramatic reduction of the AP firing frequency that may prevent neuronal death (Patel, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patel, 2004.

claim: H2O2 treatment strongly reduced neuronal excitabilities in WT GCs.
source: To investigate the role of Prmt1 in reactive oxygen species (ROS)-induced augmentation of KCNQ channel and consequential neuronal silencing, neuronal excitabilities in WT and Prmt1+/- GCs are evaluated in response to H2O2.Consistent with previous studies (Gamper et al., 2006), H2O2 treatment strongly reduced neuronal excitabilities in WT GCs (Figure 8a–b).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings from WT granule cells before and after H2O2 treatment, with results shown in Figure 8a-b.

claim: The AP firing rate during injection of a 200 pA depolarizing current was 9.3 ± 2.1 Hz, and decreased to 1.4 ± 0.9 Hz after H2O2 treatment in WT neurons.
source: The AP firing rate during injection of a 200 pA depolarizing current was 9.3 ± 2.1 Hz, and decreased to 1.4 ± 0.9 Hz (Figure 8c, Figure 8—source data 1) after H2O2 treatment.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of action potential frequency before and after H2O2 treatment in WT neurons, with results shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The input resistance was decreased from 163.8 ± 24.9 to 116.3 ± 21.8 MΩ after H2O2 treatment in WT neurons.
source: Consistent with the KCNQ current augmentation, the input resistance was decreased from 163.8 ± 24.9 to 116.3 ± 21.8 MΩ (Figure 8d, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by input resistance measurements before and after H2O2 treatment in WT neurons, with results shown in Figure 8d.

claim: H2O2 application did not lower firing rates and input resistance in GCs of Prmt1+/- mice.
source: In contrast, H2O2 application did not lower firing rates and input resistance in GCs of Prmt1+/- mice, although their firing rates and input resistance were elevated compared to WT (Figure 8e–h, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings from Prmt1+/- granule cells before and after H2O2 treatment, with results shown in Figure 8e-h.

claim: The pharmacological inhibition of arginine methylation with MTA blocked neuronal silencing and input resistance reduction in WT GCs in response to the oxidative stress inflicted by H2O2.
source: Consistently, the pharmacological inhibition of arginine methylation with MTA (Figure 8i–l, Figure 8—source data 1) or furamidine (Figure 8m–p, Figure 8—source data 1) also blocked neuronal silencing and input resistance reduction in WT GCs in response to the oxidative stress inflicted by H2O2.
evidence: Supported by current-clamp recordings from MTA- or furamidine-treated WT granule cells before and after H2O2 treatment, with results shown in Figure 8i-p.

claim: Prmt1-mediated protein arginine methylation is necessary for ROS-induced neuronal silencing via KCNQ channel activation.
source: These data indicate that Prmt1-mediated protein arginine methylation is necessary for ROS-induced neuronal silencing via KCNQ channel activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of Prmt1 blocks H2O2-induced neuronal silencing.

claim: H2O2 induced a sharp augmentation of WT KCNQ2 channels heterologously expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Gamper et al., 2006), H2O2 induced a sharp augmentation of WT KCNQ2 channels heterologously expressed in HEK293T cells (Figure 9a).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing KCNQ2 before and after H2O2 treatment, with results shown in Figure 9a.

claim: The mean current augmentation induced by 500 μM H2O2 was 2.6 ± 0.2-fold.
source: The mean current augmentation induced by 500 μM H2O2 was 2.6 ± 0.2-fold (Figure 9h).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of H2O2-induced current augmentation, with results shown in Figure 9h.

claim: At the concentration of 500 μM, the H2O2 effect usually reached a plateau within 7~8 min of application.
source: At the concentration of 500 μM, the H2O2 effect usually reached a plateau within 7~8 min of application.
evidence: Supported by time-course analysis of H2O2-induced current augmentation.

claim: The H2O2 effect was completely reversed by the addition of a reducing agent, dithiothreitol (DTT, 2 mM), suggesting that this effect is due to a reversible oxidative modification.
source: The H2O2 effect was completely reversed by the addition of a reducing agent, dithiothreitol (DTT, 2 mM), suggesting that this effect is due to a reversible oxidative modification.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings showing reversal of H2O2-induced current augmentation upon DTT application.

claim: DTT-reduced KCNQ2 currents in H2O2-treated cells were back to the resting level within several minutes, but did not inhibit them further.
source: Notably, DTT-reduced KCNQ2 currents in H2O2-treated cells were back to the resting level within several minutes, but did not inhibit them further (Figure 9a).
evidence: Supported by time-course analysis of current recovery after DTT application, with results shown in Figure 9a.

claim: DTT had no effect on KCNQ2 currents in non-H2O2-treated cells.
source: Also, DTT had no effect on KCNQ2 currents in non- H2O2-treated cells (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by control experiments showing no effect of DTT alone on KCNQ2 currents.

claim: When protein arginine methylation was blocked with the treatment of MTA or furamidine, KCNQ2 channels appeared to be insensitive to H2O2.
source: When protein arginine methylation was blocked with the treatment of MTA (Figure 9b) or furamidine (Figure 9c), KCNQ2 channels appeared to be insensitive to H2O2 with the currents augmented by H2O2 (500 μM) by 0.9 ± 0.02-fold and 0.8 ± 0.03-fold, respectively (Figure 9h, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing KCNQ2 pretreated with methyltransferase inhibitors, with results shown in Figure 9b, c, and h.

claim: The mutant channels were insensitive to H2O2, compared to WT KCNQ2.
source: We then examined whether the sensitivity to H2O2 is abrogated by the KCNQ2 mutants with reduced methylation. As shown in Figure 9d–g, the mutant channels were insensitive to H2O2, compared to WT KCNQ2.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing mutant KCNQ2 channels, with results shown in Figure 9d-g.

claim: Currents of the R333K, R345K, R353K and R435K mutant channels were augmented by 1.6 ± 0.3-, 0.9 ± 0.1-, 0.7 ± 0.1- and 1.1 ± 0.1-fold, respectively, by H2O2.
source: Currents of the R333K, R345K, R353K and R435K mutant channels were augmented by 1.6 ± 0.3-, 0.9 ± 0.1-, 0.7 ± 0.1- and 1.1 ± 0.1-fold, respectively (Figure 9h, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of H2O2-induced current augmentation in mutant channels, with results shown in Figure 9h.

claim: A triple cysteine pocket in the S2-S3 linker is critical for the H2O2-induced enhancement of KCNQ channel.
source: Recently, Gamper et al. (Gamper et al., 2006) showed that a triple cysteine pocket in the S2-S3 linker is critical for the H2O2-induced enhancement of KCNQ channel.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamper et al., 2006.

claim: MTA and furamidine reduced activities of the triple-Cys mutant of KCNQ2 by a similar extent as it did those of the WT KCNQ2 channel, while the mutant was insensitive to H2O2 as expected.
source: Interestingly, MTA and furamidine reduced activities of the triple-Cys mutant of KCNQ2 by a similar extent as it did those of the WT KCNQ2 channel, while the mutant was insensitive to H2O2 as expected (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch clamp recordings from HEK293T cells expressing triple-Cys mutant KCNQ2, with results shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The H2O2 activation pathway is unnecessary for the arginine methylation-mediated regulation of Prmt1.
source: This result indicates that the H2O2 activation pathway is unnecessary for the arginine methylation-mediated regulation of Prmt1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that methylation inhibitors reduce activity of both WT and triple-Cys mutant KCNQ2, while only WT is sensitive to H2O2.

claim: Prmt1 is prerequisite for cytoprotective enhancement of KCNQ currents in the milieu of oxidative stress.
source: Taken together, Prmt1 is prerequisite for cytoprotective enhancement of KCNQ currents in the milieu of oxidative stress.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that Prmt1 deficiency or inhibition blocks H2O2-induced KCNQ current augmentation and neuronal silencing.

claim: The heterozygous reduction of the Prmt1 gene dose in mice caused spontaneous seizures.
source: In this study, we describe a novel regulatory mechanism whereby methylation of KCNQ2 affects KCNQ/M channel activities and overall excitabilities of the brain. The heterozygous reduction of the Prmt1 gene dose in mice caused spontaneous seizures.
evidence: Supported by EEG recording data from Prmt1+/- mice showing spontaneous seizure activity.

claim: The elevated neuronal excitability in Prmt1+/- mice appears to be a direct result of reduced KCNQ/M channel activities in that KCNQ2 from the Prmt1+/- brain was less asymmetrically methylated and showed diminished affinity to PIP2.
source: The elevated neuronal excitability in Prmt1+/- mice appears to be a direct result of reduced KCNQ/M channel activities in that KCNQ2 from the Prmt1+/- brain was less asymmetrically methylated and showed diminished affinity to PIP2.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced KCNQ2 methylation, reduced M-currents, and increased excitability in Prmt1+/- mice.

claim: The activation of KCNQ channel under oxidative stress as well as its basal activity at rest depends on protein arginine methylation.
source: Furthermore, the activation of KCNQ channel under oxidative stress as well as its basal activity at rest depends on protein arginine methylation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that methylation regulates both basal KCNQ activity and H2O2-induced augmentation.

claim: ROS generated under oxidative stress induces augmentation of KCNQ currents in neurons.
source: It is well known that ROS generated under oxidative stress induces augmentation of KCNQ currents in neurons (Gamper et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamper et al., 2006.

claim: The resulting reduction in neuronal discharge lowers electrical activity of the cell and energy consumption, thereby providing an important mechanism of protecting neurons from the oxidative stress-induced death.
source: The resulting reduction in neuronal discharge lowers electrical activity of the cell and energy consumption, thereby providing an important mechanism of protecting neurons from the oxidative stress-induced death (Gamper et al., 2006; Won et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gamper et al., 2006; Won et al., 2002.

claim: Oxidative stress is involved in induction of seizures.
source: Considering that oxidative stress is also involved in induction of seizures (Patel, 2004), the impairment of neuroprotective KCNQ activation in response to oxidative stress, may contribute to spontaneous seizures together with the reduced basal activity of KCNQ channels in Prmt1+/- mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Patel, 2004.

claim: The impairment of neuroprotective KCNQ activation in response to oxidative stress may contribute to spontaneous seizures together with the reduced basal activity of KCNQ channels in Prmt1+/- mice.
source: Considering that oxidative stress is also involved in induction of seizures (Patel, 2004), the impairment of neuroprotective KCNQ activation in response to oxidative stress, may contribute to spontaneous seizures together with the reduced basal activity of KCNQ channels in Prmt1+/- mice.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the combined observations of impaired H2O2 response and seizures in Prmt1+/- mice.

claim: Protein arginine methylation is a unique post-translational modification that increases the KCNQ/M channel function unlike other known regulatory signaling pathways.
source: Protein arginine methylation is a unique post-translational modification that increases the KCNQ/M channel function unlike other known regulatory signaling pathways, and thus provides a platform for the design of novel therapeutic strategies for epilepsy and other neuronal hyperexcitability disorders.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that methylation increases KCNQ activity, in contrast to other known regulatory mechanisms that decrease activity.

claim: All of the methylation sites reside within the C-terminal PIP2 binding domain.
source: Our results find that 4 arginine residues (R333, R345, R353, and R435) are the major methylation sites in KCNQ2. Interestingly, all of the methylation sites reside within the C-terminal PIP2 binding domain.
evidence: Based on mass spectrometry identification of methylation sites and known structural information about KCNQ2 PIP2-binding domain.

claim: The C-terminal PIP2 binding domain serves as binding sites for multiple signaling molecules as well as PIP2.
source: This is known as a 'hot spot', as it serves as binding sites for multiple signaling molecules as well as PIP2 (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Hernandez et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delmas and Brown, 2005; Hernandez et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2003.

claim: Decreased methylation lowers PIP2 affinity.
source: The observation that decreased methylation lowers PIP2 affinity proposes that Prmt1 methylation on the arginine residues would increase channel-PIP2 interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations of reduced PIP2 affinity in methylation-deficient mutants.

claim: Methylation renders the guanidinium of arginines to be more electron-rich and thus to exhibit higher pKa values.
source: Indeed, previous computational analyses revealed that methylation renders the guanidinium of arginines to be more electron-rich and thus to exhibit higher pKa values (Shearer, 2008), which would stabilize the positive charge of the arginine residue in proteins in the physiological condition and thereby likely facilitate their electrostatic interaction with negatively charged molecules.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shearer, 2008.

claim: Arginine methylation is required for the KCNQ channel activity because it promotes electrostatic binding of KCNQ proteins to PIP2.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that arginine methylation is required for the KCNQ channel activity because it promotes electrostatic binding of KCNQ proteins to PIP2.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced PIP2 affinity in methylation-deficient mutants and computational predictions about methylation effects on arginine charge.

claim: Various KCNQ channel mutations associated with epilepsy have been shown to cause a reduction in M-channel activity, which all can lead to membrane depolarization and increased neuronal firing via diverse mechanisms.
source: Various KCNQ channel mutations associated with epilepsy have been shown to cause a reduction in M-channel activity, which all can lead to membrane depolarization and increased neuronal firing via diverse mechanisms.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple studies of epilepsy-associated KCNQ mutations.

claim: Mutations in the C-terminal region of KCNQ channels reduce channel activities by interfering with channel targeting to the surface membrane, protein stability, interaction with calmodulin, or modulation by cAMP.
source: Mutations in the C-terminal region of KCNQ channels reduce channel activities by interfering with channel targeting to the surface membrane (Schwake et al., 2000), protein stability (Soldovieri et al., 2006), interaction with calmodulin (Jentsch, 2000), or modulation by cAMP (Schroeder et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwake et al., 2000; Soldovieri et al., 2006; Jentsch, 2000; Schroeder et al., 1998.

claim: Mutations affecting the pore region of KCNQ2 may reduce currents by affecting ion channel conductance, while mutations at the S4 domain affect channel gating and increase the threshold for channel activation.
source: Mutations affecting the pore region of KCNQ2 may reduce currents by affecting ion channel conductance, while mutations at the S4 domain affect channel gating and increase the threshold for channel activation (Maljevic et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maljevic et al., 2010.

claim: R353G, a mutant of one of the major methylation sites identified in this study, is linked to familial epilepsy, likely due to reduced calmodulin binding and a consequent defect in membrane trafficking.
source: It is interesting in this context that R353G, a mutant of one of the major methylation sites identified in this study, is linked to familial epilepsy, likely due to reduced calmodulin binding and a consequent defect in membrane trafficking (Jentsch, 2000; Etxeberria et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jentsch, 2000; Etxeberria et al., 2008.

claim: A recent study proposed an additional pathophysiological mechanism involving a diminished PIP2 affinity of the channel for the R353G epileptic KCNQ2 mutation.
source: However, a recent study proposed an additional pathophysiological mechanism involving a diminished PIP2 affinity of the channel for this epileptic KCNQ2 mutation (Kosenko et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kosenko et al., 2012.

claim: Disruption of KCNQ2 channel-PIP2 interaction caused by decreased methylation is a key mechanism linked to neuronal hyperactivity.
source: This is in agreement with our current study indicating that disruption of KCNQ2 channel-PIP2 interaction caused by decreased methylation is a key mechanism linked to neuronal hyperactivity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing that reduced methylation decreases PIP2 affinity and increases neuronal excitability.

claim: KCNQ3 channel contains conserved methylation sites within the PIP2 biding domain.
source: Like KCNQ2, KCNQ3 channel contains conserved methylation sites within the PIP2 biding domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) suggesting that arginine methylation might be also involved in regulation of channel-PIP2 interaction in KCNQ3 channels as well.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis showing conserved arginine residues in KCNQ3, with results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Arginine methylation might be involved in regulation of channel-PIP2 interaction in KCNQ3 channels.
source: Like KCNQ2, KCNQ3 channel contains conserved methylation sites within the PIP2 biding domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) suggesting that arginine methylation might be also involved in regulation of channel-PIP2 interaction in KCNQ3 channels as well.
evidence: Speculative inference based on sequence conservation of methylation sites in KCNQ3.

claim: The KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 complex produces M-currents.
source: Considering that the KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 complex produces M-currents, hypo-methylation of either KCNQs might significantly diminish M-currents and neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: Based on established knowledge that KCNQ2/3 heteromers form M-currents.

claim: Hypo-methylation of either KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 might significantly diminish M-currents and neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: Considering that the KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 complex produces M-currents, hypo-methylation of either KCNQs might significantly diminish M-currents and neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the heteromeric nature of M-channels and conservation of methylation sites.

claim: The positively charged arginines are important for electrostatic interaction with PIP2 in other PIP2-sensitive channels and transporters such as Kir2 and GIRK.
source: The positively charged arginines are also important for electrostatic interaction with PIP2 in other PIP2-sensitive channels and transporters such as Kir2 (Hansen et al., 2011; Huang et al., 1998; Lopes et al., 2002), and GIRK (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2011; Huang et al., 1998; Lopes et al., 2002; Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011.

claim: PIP2 is required for proper function of many plasma membrane ion channels and transporters.
source: PIP2 is required for proper function of many plasma membrane ion channels and transporters (Suh and Hille, 2008; Hilgemann et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Suh and Hille, 2008; Hilgemann et al., 2001.

claim: Methylation can be a general mechanism for regulating ion flux physiology.
source: Thus, methylation can be a general mechanism for regulating ion flux physiology.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the widespread importance of PIP2 in ion channel regulation and the potential for methylation to modulate PIP2 interactions.

claim: The effects of KCNQ channel block on firing rates are not the same as those of Prmt1 block, implying a possible involvement of other Prmt1 target(s) in neuronal hyperexcitability and seizures.
source: Consistent with this, our results show that the effects of KCNQ channel block on firing rates are not the same as those of Prmt1 block (Figure 3), implying a possible involvement of other Prmt1 target(s) in neuronal hyperexcitability and seizures.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that XE991 effects differ between WT and Prmt1+/- neurons, suggesting additional Prmt1 targets beyond KCNQ.

claim: SK and BK channels are not involved in the incomplete recovery of excitability by PIP2 loading.
source: PIP2 loading to Prmt1+/- GCs recovered the firing properties significantly but incompletely. It appears that SK and BK channels are not involved in this matter.
evidence: Inferred from the experiments using SK and BK channel blockers showing no contribution to hyperexcitability.

claim: The results provide the first direct evidence of functional role for protein arginine methylation in the control of neuronal excitability.
source: Regardless, the results presented here provide the first direct evidence of functional role for protein arginine methylation in the control of neuronal excitability and also offers a platform to further investigate the physiological and pathophysiological roles of KCNQ/M channel activity in CNS.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results demonstrating that Prmt1-mediated methylation regulates KCNQ channels and neuronal excitability.

claim: Prmt1 homozygous knockout mice are embryonic lethal.
source: As Prmt1 homozygous knockout mice are embryonic lethal (Choi et al., 2012), we used heterozygous mice (Prmt1+/-) for our study.
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2012.

claim: KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 are the earliest identified K+ channels associated with idiopathic epilepsy.
source: Together with KCNA1, KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 are the earliest identified K+ channels associated with idiopathic epilepsy (Rogawski, 2000; Schroeder et al., 1998; Browne et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rogawski, 2000; Schroeder et al., 1998; Browne et al., 1994.

claim: More than 30 mutations have been detected in KCNQ channels, most of which were found in KCNQ2: only four mutations were found in KCNQ3.
source: More than 30 mutations have been detected in KCNQ channels, most of which were found in KCNQ2: only four mutations were found in KCNQ3 (Maljevic et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maljevic et al., 2010.

claim: KCNQ channel mutations caused a reduction in channel activity by different molecular mechanisms, by which all can lead to membrane depolarization and increased neuronal firing.
source: These mutations caused a reduction in channel activity by different molecular mechanisms, by which all can lead to membrane depolarization and increased neuronal firing.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from studies of epilepsy-associated KCNQ mutations.

claim: Heteromeric KCNQ2/3 potassium channels form the M-current, a subthreshold potassium current.
source: In the central nervous system (CNS), heteromeric KCNQ2/3 potassium channels form the M-current, a subthreshold potassium current (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Jentsch, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delmas and Brown, 2005; Jentsch, 2000.

claim: Due to the slow gating kinetics, M-currents effectively oppose sustained membrane depolarization and repetitive action potential (AP) firing.
source: Due to the slow gating kinetics, M-currents effectively oppose sustained membrane depolarization and repetitive action potential (AP) firing (Brown and Passmore, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Passmore, 2009.

claim: Breakdown of M-channels by loss of function mutations or pharmacological inhibitors leads to neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: Thus, breakdown of M-channels by loss of function mutations or pharmacological inhibitors leads to neuronal hyperexcitability (Schroeder et al., 1998; Delmas and Brown, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schroeder et al., 1998; Delmas and Brown, 2005.

claim: KCNQ potassium channels are both mutated in human epilepsy and principal targets of an approved anti-epileptic drug (ezogabine/retigabine).
source: KCNQ potassium channels are standouts for epileptologists, in that they are both mutated in human epilepsy and principal targets of an approved anti-epileptic drug (ezogabine/retigabine) (Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Soldovieri et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Soldovieri et al., 2011.

claim: M-channels are inhibited by muscarinic acetylcholine receptor agonists, leading to a profound increase in cellular excitability that can be reversed by the withdrawal of receptor agonist.
source: Notably, M-channels are inhibited by muscarinic acetylcholine receptor agonists, leading to a profound increase in cellular excitability that can be reversed by the withdrawal of receptor agonist.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of M-channel regulation by muscarinic receptors.

claim: Some subtypes of receptors for dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, and several peptide neurotransmitters, including luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone and bradykinin, are capable of inhibiting the M-channels.
source: Some subtypes of receptors for dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, and several peptide neurotransmitters, including luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone and bradykinin, are also found to be capable of inhibiting the M-channels.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of M-channel regulation by various neurotransmitter receptors.

claim: M-channels require membrane phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to open.
source: An important property of M-channels is that they require membrane phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to open (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Suh and Hille, 2008), and the certain receptors mentioned above suppress M-current by depletion of PIP2 (Delmas and Brown, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delmas and Brown, 2005; Suh and Hille, 2008.

claim: Certain receptors suppress M-current by depletion of PIP2.
source: An important property of M-channels is that they require membrane phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to open (Delmas and Brown, 2005; Suh and Hille, 2008), and the certain receptors mentioned above suppress M-current by depletion of PIP2 (Delmas and Brown, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Delmas and Brown, 2005.

claim: M-channels are inhibited by CaM in a Ca2+-dependent manner, providing another mode of intracellular modulation of M-channel activities.
source: In addition, M-channels are also inhibited by CaM in a Ca2+-dependent manner, providing another mode of intracellular modulation of M-channel activities (Gamper and Shapiro, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamper and Shapiro, 2003.

claim: Protein kinase C (PKC) phosphorylation of the KCNQ2 subunit reduces the affinity for its PIP2 binding and activities.
source: Recent work indicates that protein kinase C (PKC) phosphorylation of the KCNQ2 subunit reduces the affinity for its PIP2 binding and activities (Kosenko et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kosenko et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Sumoylation of KCNQ channels results in reduced channel activity.
source: Likewise, sumoylation of KCNQ channels results in reduced channel activity (Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qi et al., 2014.

claim: All regulatory pathways discovered so far act on the KCNQ channels to reduce the channel activity and increase neuronal excitability.
source: Thus, all regulatory pathways discovered so far act on the KCNQ channels to reduce the channel activity and increase neuronal excitability.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple studies of KCNQ channel regulation.

claim: To date there is no evidence supporting regulatory mechanisms to increase the channel-PIP2 interaction and channel activities.
source: Given its important role in stabilization of neuronal excitability, there has been much speculation for regulatory mechanisms to increase the channel-PIP2 interaction and channel activities, however, to date there is no evidence supporting such regulatory mechanism.
evidence: Based on the absence of prior evidence in the literature for positive regulation of KCNQ-PIP2 interaction.
