claim: Protein methylation, along with phosphorylation, controls a variety of cellular functions.
source: Protein methylation, along with phosphorylation, controls a variety of cellular functions (Nicholson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicholson et al., 2009.

claim: Protein arginine methyltransferases (Prmts) are enzymes that catalyze the transfer of a methyl group to arginine residues of histone or non-histone substrates.
source: Protein arginine methyltransferases (Prmts) are enzymes that catalyze the transfer of a methyl group to arginine residues of histone or non-histone substrates (Boisvert et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boisvert et al., 2005.

claim: In mammals, nine Prmts have been characterized.
source: In mammals, nine Prmts have been characterized.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the Prmt family.

claim: Prmt1, originally identified as a histone H4 methyltransferase, methylates many non-histone proteins and implicated in diverse cellular processes including RNA processing, transcriptional regulation, oncogenesis, cell survival, insulin signaling, and metabolism.
source: Among these, Prmt1, originally identified as a histone H4 methyltransferase, methylates many non-histone proteins and implicated in diverse cellular processes including RNA processing, transcriptional regulation, oncogenesis, cell survival, insulin signaling, and metabolism (Boisvert et al., 2005; Bedford and Clarke, 2009; Krause et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boisvert et al., 2005; Bedford and Clarke, 2009; Krause et al., 2007.

claim: Prmt1 is a predominant Prmt in mammalian cells and is highly expressed in the CNS.
source: Although Prmt1 is a predominant Prmt in mammalian cells and is highly expressed in the CNS (Nicholson et al., 2009; Bedford and Clarke, 2009), its functional significance in the CNS has not yet been identified.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nicholson et al., 2009; Bedford and Clarke, 2009.

claim: The functional significance of Prmt1 in the CNS has not yet been identified.
source: Although Prmt1 is a predominant Prmt in mammalian cells and is highly expressed in the CNS (Nicholson et al., 2009; Bedford and Clarke, 2009), its functional significance in the CNS has not yet been identified.
evidence: Based on the absence of prior evidence in the literature for CNS-specific functions of Prmt1.

claim: The positively charged (basic) arginines or lysines are candidates for mediating electrostatic interaction with PIP2 in channels such as KCNQ, Kir2, and GIRK.
source: The positively charged (basic) arginines or lysines are candidates for mediating electrostatic interaction with PIP2 in channels such as KCNQ (Hernandez et al., 2008), Kir2 (Hansen et al., 2011; Huang et al., 1998; Lopes et al., 2002), and GIRK (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hernandez et al., 2008; Hansen et al., 2011; Huang et al., 1998; Lopes et al., 2002; Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011.

claim: Each additional methyl group to an arginine residue can readily modulate their physical properties.
source: Considering that each additional methyl group to an arginine residue can readily modulate their physical properties (Bedford and Clarke, 2009), methylation of arginine residues in PIP2 binding domain may alter KCNQ channels' affinity for PIP2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bedford and Clarke, 2009.

claim: It is not known whether methylation of arginine residues in PIP2 binding domain really occurs and regulates the channel activity and whether it is implicated in common disease phenotypes.
source: However it is not known whether such methylation really occurs and regulates the channel activity and whether it is implicated in common disease phenotypes.
evidence: Based on the absence of prior evidence in the literature for methylation-dependent regulation of KCNQ-PIP2 interaction.

claim: Prmt1-dependent facilitation of KCNQ-PIP2 interaction underlies the positive regulation of KCNQ activity by arginine methylation.
source: Collectively, we propose that Prmt1-dependent facilitation of KCNQ-PIP2 interaction underlies the positive regulation of KCNQ activity by arginine methylation, which may serve as a key target for prevention of neuronal hyperexcitability and seizures.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing that Prmt1 methylation increases KCNQ-PIP2 interaction and channel activity.

claim: Prmt1-dependent regulation of KCNQ channels represents an important mechanism of neuronal protection against over-excitability.
source: We propose that Prmt1-dependent regulation of KCNQ channels represents an important mechanism of neuronal protection against over-excitability.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing that Prmt1 regulates KCNQ channels and neuronal excitability, with implications for seizure prevention.
